claims.text: At stage-2 CancelOrderAsync called order.Cancel(), then notifier.Send (QueuedNotifier adds a pending notifications row to the DbContext), then one SaveChangesAsync that wrote both.

At stage-3 CancelOrderAsync calls repository.FindAsync, order.Cancel(), events.DispatchAsync(order), repository.SaveChangesAsync() in that order and no longer calls notifier.Send; events is a DomainEventDispatcher received through OrderService's constructor.

DomainEventDispatcher takes one IEnumerable<IDomainEventHandler<T>> per event kind; DispatchAsync loops over order.DomainEvents, switches on type, awaits each HandleAsync in turn, then calls order.ClearDomainEvents(); a new kind needs one more parameter and case.
IDomainEventHandler<in TEvent> where TEvent : IDomainEvent declares one method, Task HandleAsync(TEvent domainEvent).

Two handlers are registered for OrderCancelled: NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents (implements the interface for all six kinds Order records, one HandleAsync each; adds an outbox_messages row via IOutbox) and RecordOrderStatusHistory (adds an order_status_history row); neither saves.

EfOutbox and RecordOrderStatusHistory both add to the injected scoped DonHangDbContext, the same instance EfOrderRepository uses within a request, so OrderService's one SaveChangesAsync writes the order's change and both rows.

claims.text: AddDbContext registers the DbContext with a scoped lifetime by default, so in ASP.NET Core every class resolved in one request shares the same instance.

claims.text: SaveChangesAsync, when no transaction is open, wraps all changes it writes in one database transaction: either all are applied or, on failure, none are.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Saving Data — Transactions (default transaction behavior)

claims.text: SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync writes every change the DbContext tracks at that moment, and only it writes them; if never called, nothing tracked is written. So a handler saving the shared context would also write the order's cancel.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Saving Data — Basic Save; Change Tracking overview

claims.text: An exception thrown from an awaited HandleAsync propagates out of DispatchAsync and out of CancelOrderAsync, so the following SaveChangesAsync line is not executed.

claims.text: Resolving IEnumerable<T> from the .NET DI container returns an instance of every service registered for T, in registration order, so NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents (ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:31) runs before RecordOrderStatusHistory (:37).

claims.text: AddDonHangInfrastructure, which DonHang.Api's Program.cs calls to register the infrastructure classes the order use cases need, registers each of the six event interfaces once for NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents and once for RecordOrderStatusHistory (AddScoped), then DomainEventDispatcher.

Every use case in OrderService at stage-3 (PlaceOrderAsync, CancelOrderAsync, ShipOrderAsync, RequestRefundAsync, CompleteRefundAsync, FailRefundAsync) calls events.DispatchAsync(order) immediately before repository.SaveChangesAsync().

At stage-3 the IOutbox row is saved with the order and passed on only after the save (OutboxRelay, a hosted service in DonHang.Api); NotificationSender now runs in DonHang.Notifications, a separate program, and emails Mailpit; the API answers without waiting for the email.

claims.text: NotifyCustomerOnOrderEvents throws InvalidOperationException when the order's customer is not found by ICustomerRepository.FindAsync.

A handler that calls another program over the network cannot undo that call if the later save fails; keeping handlers to rows in the same DbContext is this module's choice. Opposing view, stated in the lesson: designs that need such calls run them after the save.

Adding a reaction as a new handler plus one registration leaves Order and CancelOrderAsync unchanged, which is the Open/Closed Principle applied; it holds for new reactions, not for new event kinds (new constructor parameter and case).
